html:
The Epic of Gilgamesh is a long poem from ancient Mesopotamia about Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, and his search for fame and then for eternal life. It is the oldest great work of literature that survives.

It grew over many centuries. Separate Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh may date to the court of Ur III, around 2100 BCE. In the Old Babylonian period, around the eighteenth century BCE, they were joined into one epic in Akkadian. The best known version, in twelve tablets, was edited later and is credited to a scribe named Sin-leqi-unninni.

The story:

  • Gilgamesh is a proud, harsh king. The gods make a wild man, Enkidu, as his match, and the two become close friends.
  • Together they kill the monster Humbaba in the Cedar Forest and the Bull of Heaven.
  • The gods punish them by making Enkidu sicken and die. Gilgamesh, terrified of death, wanders to find Utnapishtim, the one man the gods made immortal after a great flood.
  • He fails to win immortality, loses a plant of youth to a snake, and returns home to look at the walls of Uruk, his lasting work.

The best copies were found in the Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, written in cuneiform. In 1872 George Smith read the flood story to an astonished London audience: it closely matches the flood of Noah in the Bible, and is older.
sum: The Epic of Gilgamesh is a long poem from ancient Mesopotamia about Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, and his search for fame and then for eternal life. It is the oldest great work of literature that survives.
